intuition: A word must match both a beginning and an ending. Store paths combining each possible suffix, a separator, and the full word. A query follows suffix + separator + prefix. Save the latest word index along each path so matching queries return the largest index.

For each word, insert every suffix followed by a separator and then the full word into a trie. A query for suffix suff and prefix pref follows suff + separator + pref. The separator fixes where the suffix ends, while the trailing traversal only needs to match the beginning of the full word.
Prefix and suffix may overlap in the original word; this representation still works because the stored sequence deliberately contains a suffix followed by a full copy of the word.

Each visited trie node remembers the current word’s index. Insert words in increasing index order so later matching words overwrite earlier indices automatically. The final query node therefore contains the largest matching index, including when duplicate words appear. A missing character edge proves no stored suffix-and-prefix combination fits.
The separator must be outside the lowercase alphabet, so it cannot be confused with actual word characters.

The insertion loop includes start=len(word), yielding the extra sequence "{" + word for an empty suffix. Current query constraints require a nonempty suffix, so no legal query starts along this extra branch. Its presence is harmless and keeps the suffix-listing all possibilities loop simple; it would also support empty suffixes if the interface were extended.
The separator is essential: matching a suffix must reach it exactly, whereas the prefix portion may stop before the full word ends.

steps: The example constructs WordFilter from ["apple"], whose only index is 0.
One stored sequence is "e{apple", generated from the suffix beginning at the final character.
The query pref="a", suff="e" becomes the traversal sequence "e{a".
Follow the e edge, then the separator edge, then a. Each of these nodes was visited by the insertion for word index 0.
The final node stores 0, so return 0. A query starting with an absent suffix or prefix would stop early with -1.

codeNotes.note: Combining an exact suffix and a full-word prefix makes the two independent conditions searchable as one trie path.
Increasing-index insertion overwrites the stored answer at every matching path, directly maintaining the largest index.
The query stops after its prefix rather than needing the complete word; the reached node already summarizes all longer matching words.

keyDecision: The separator keeps the suffix and prefix parts distinct. Store increasing word indices so the latest one wins.

concept.question: How can one letter path enforce both a word’s ending and beginning?
intuition: Filtering all words for each prefix-and-suffix query repeats the same comparisons. Build an index whose paths encode both conditions together.

For each word, store every suffix followed by a special separator and then the full word. A query follows its suffix, the separator, and its prefix. Save the greatest matching word index along each path.
concept.observation: The separator fixes the complete suffix boundary; the following letters need only match the beginning of the word.
approach: Insert suffix–separator–word paths for every indexed word.
Record the latest word index at every visited prefix node.
Follow suffix–separator–prefix for a query, or fail at a missing letter.
concept.correctness: A stored combined path reaches a query endpoint exactly when its suffix portion equals the requested full suffix and its full-word portion begins with the requested prefix. Thus traversal matches both conditions simultaneously. Increasing-index insertion leaves the largest matching index at every endpoint, giving the required tie result.

complexity.explanation: A word of maximum length supplies linearly many suffix paths, each linear in length, making construction and index storage quadratic in that length per word. A query walks only its suffix and prefix lengths.

pitfalls: The separator fixes the complete suffix boundary; the following letters need only match the beginning of the word.
The separator must not be a permitted word letter.
